body: Eleven lampposts down the long side of the park, and he counts them every time, because counting is the thing that gets him round. He is fifty-eight. He has walked this loop four mornings a week since March, when a doctor put a number in front of him and did not say very much afterwards. It is twenty to seven and wet, and it was wet on Tuesday as well. The dog people nod at him and he nods back, and that is the whole of the social content. In the fifth week he notices, going up to the second floor at work, that he is not stopping on the landing any more.

Nothing about that is silly and nothing about it is vanity. A man was told his body was in trouble and he did something about it, four mornings a week, in the rain, for months. Whatever taught him to take that seriously deserves the credit for it.

It is worth saying that plainly at the start, because the argument that follows is a criticism and criticisms of this subject curdle very quickly into a sneer at people who are only trying to get better.

Here is the awkward part. The Church has an unhelpful history with the body. For long stretches it treated physical life as the lower floor — tolerated, disciplined, occasionally despised — and taught, mostly by implication, that the serious part of a person was elsewhere. That is closer to Greek philosophy than to a text which spends chapters on food, on rest, on skin conditions, on what to do with a body after a birth, and which puts a weekly command to stop working near the top of a very short list. A subject that central was left largely unattended for a very long time, and things do not stay unattended.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, 46 of them on air. A frequency for this, HM 377.60, Inspire Wellness, is assigned and in build and has not opened yet, and so is most of the sleep and rest stretch beside it.

Holding a frequency for the body without turning it into either a health programme or a rebuke is harder than it sounds, and it is the reason that stretch is being built slowly rather than filled. Nothing on it may promise a result. Nothing on it may imply that a listener who is unwell has been doing something wrong. What is left after those two rules is narrower and quieter than the market usually allows, and it is the only version worth broadcasting. One of these says look after the body because it is not yours. The other says perfect the body because it is all there is.

Into that long vacancy walked the wellness industry, and the first thing to say about it is that it did good work. It got sedentary people moving. It made sleep a respectable thing to protect. It got men who would not say the word depression to a doctor talking about their heads at all. It took a subject the Church had put down and treated it as though it mattered, which it does. Nobody should pretend that was nothing.

But it built something with the full apparatus of a faith around it, and mostly without noticing. There is a moral vocabulary — clean, toxic, pure, and the word guilty attached to a biscuit. There are disciplines, kept daily and recorded. There is confession, in the form of telling people what you have eaten. There is a promise of transformation, and there is an implied verdict for those who do not achieve it. All of it aimed at an object which is, in the end, going to fail.
That last point is not a debating trick. It is the whole of the difficulty.

Be fair to the alternative before pressing on it, because it answers a real question well. What should I do this morning? Move, eat something that is food, go to bed. That is better advice than most people were getting, and a person who follows it will be better off. But push the frame to the place everyone eventually arrives at and it has nothing to say. Illness becomes a verdict on the person who has it, ageing becomes a defeat rather than a season, and the body’s eventual failure — universal, scheduled, arriving for the disciplined and the undisciplined alike — has no meaning available except loss of control. A system that can only speak to bodies while they are winning is not a system for bodies.
The one thing everybody has in common is the part it cannot discuss.

A woman of thirty-nine is in a waiting room at half past four with a magazine she is not reading. She ran. She slept eight hours most nights and was smug about it. She cooked from scratch on Sundays for the week and her colleagues used to comment on it. She has an illness now that nobody caused, and she has had it for eleven months. Her phone buzzes and it is a good friend, and the message is a link with a note saying it might be worth cutting out seed oils, just in case. She reads it twice, puts the phone in her bag face down, and goes back to the magazine. She does not reply that evening or at all.
The friend meant nothing but kindness. She had no vocabulary available that lets her offer help without also implying a cause, and where illness is a verdict, every offer arrives as an accusation.

The older account has been used badly too, and it should be said flatly rather than glossed. It has been used to excuse neglect of the body, to tell exhausted people that rest is self-indulgence, to spiritualise a condition that wanted a doctor and a prescription. Believe and it will lift. Pray harder. That has done real damage to real people, some of whom are still angry about it and are entitled to be. Any defence of the older frame that skips over that has not earned a hearing.

But notice that every one of those failures is the same failure: treating the body as beneath the subject. The frame itself says the opposite. It says the body is not yours, which cuts in both directions at once — it is worth looking after, and it was never the point of you. It says rest is commanded rather than earned, which means it does not have to be deserved by a productive week. And it says the body’s decline is not a personal failing, which is the one sentence the whole apparatus of wellness structurally cannot say to anybody.

So this is not an argument for caring less about sleep and food and moving about. It is an argument about what those things are for and what happens when they run out. Look after it because it was lent to you. Rest because you were told to, not because you finished. And when it goes wrong anyway — which it will, on a timetable nobody consulted you about — you have not lost, and nobody needs to work out what you did to deserve it.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Four kinds of programming sit on this dial, and it is worth knowing they are there before you turn it. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a great deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained and prayed through rather than sung. There is family programming, safe to have on in a room with children in it. And there are the international frequencies, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them. No menu, no queue, nothing to decide before anything starts.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 301.90 — Radiant Stones Concerts. It is on air, and it is worship recorded with the room left in: other people, audible, not in time with each other, none of them optimising anything. That matters here because the wellness hour is a solitary one by design — headphones, a private routine, a number to improve, nobody else in it. What plays on this frequency is the opposite arrangement. It is a building full of people, most of whom are not well, none of whom are being measured, and all of whom are doing the same thing at once. Put it on for the loop of the park.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people reach for, which is how the next one gets built and how a stretch like the rest frequencies gets its turn.

So take this as an invitation rather than a regime. There is no programme attached to it, nothing to give up on Monday, and no plan for you to fail by Thursday. Put HM 301.90 on tomorrow morning and go and walk your eleven lampposts with it, and then go to bed at a reasonable hour because you were told to rather than because you earned it. The body is worth the trouble. It is simply not the thing you are.
